pages.metaDescription: Website design across DuPage County, IL. What actually gets built, how the first month runs, and what stays registered in your name. Plans from $250 monthly.
pages.h1: Website design in DuPage County, IL, and exactly what exists at the end of it.
pages.lede: Most of this trade sells an outcome and stays vague about the parts. This page does the opposite — the inventory, the schedule, the questions to ask us, and the two or three reasons you might be better off hiring nobody.

sections.h2: A website is not one object. It is about seven.
paras: The reason so many owners end up stuck with a provider they have stopped liking is that they only ever received one of the seven. The pages arrived. The accounts underneath them stayed somewhere else.
So a build here hands over a set of separate working pieces, each sitting in an account with your name on it rather than ours.
bullets: A domain, bought into a registrar account that belongs to you
The site itself, built page by page around what you sell rather than poured into a layout
Google Workspace email at that domain, so a reply comes from you at your own address instead of a free inbox
A calendar the booking page is permitted to write into
A Google Business Profile, verified and filled the whole way in
Service pages, which are what the local search work actually runs on
A customer list, from the week there is one worth keeping

sections.h2: The first month, in the order it genuinely happens.
paras: None of this takes a year. What takes time is waiting on somebody, so the sequence is arranged to keep as much of the waiting as possible on our side.
bullets: Week one is paperwork and it is the least interesting part — domain moved or bought into your name, email set up, the Google profile claimed or prised back from whoever has it, and an hour spent listening to how your work really arrives.
Week two the pages get written and built, with each service named the way a customer names it out loud.
Week three you read all of it and say what is wrong. Everybody has something, and this is the week that exists for it.
Week four it goes live, booking is switched on, the profile is completed properly, and the search work starts running to a schedule.

sections.h2: What we need from you, and it is less than people brace for.
paras: Owners delay this because they picture a folder of homework. In practice there are four things, and we can start with three of them.
bullets: Your prices, or an honest range plus the thing that moves it
Photographs off your own phone — the room, the work, the vehicle, you
The questions people ask on the phone before they commit
One hour, once, at the beginning, on the premises or on a call

sections.h2: Two updates a month, and what that covers in practice.
paras: It appears in every plan and it is the line owners are most suspicious of, so here is the unglamorous version. An update is a change to something that already exists: a price, an opening hour, a paragraph, a photograph, a service you have stopped offering, somebody who has left.
Send it however suits you — a text, an email, a photograph of a printed sheet with a pen mark on it. No ticket number stands between you and a paragraph, and nobody books a meeting about one.

Two is a ceiling and not a target. Plenty of months go by with one or none, and the number is really there to remove the reason a wrong price sits on a page for a year, which is the suspicion that asking will turn into an ordeal.

New work is a different thing and we name it rather than blur it. A whole new section, a shop, a second location with pages of its own — that gets quoted against the job and put in writing before anybody starts.

sections.h2: Four questions worth putting to anybody who quotes you.
paras: You are probably reading two or three of these pages this week and ours is one of them. These four separate the arrangements quickly, and we would rather you asked them of us as well.
bullets: Whose account is the domain registered in, and can I log into it today?
When I want something changed, who does it reach and how long does it take?
What is included every month, listed in nouns rather than adjectives?
What does it cost to leave, and what comes with me when I do?

sections.h2: Both prices, and the reason the term is a year.
paras: Foundation is $250 a month with a one-time $250 to build it. Growth is $500 a month with a one-time $500, and turns on the ledger underneath — invoicing, card payments, the automatic messages, expenses, monthly reports and the accounting sync.

Twelve months settled at once removes 15 percent, so the year lands at $2,550 or $5,100 and the build stays on a line of its own. Two extras can sit on top of either plan: phone answering around the clock at $100 a month, automated Google review replies at $130.

The term is twelve months because roughly the first three of them pass before a new site pays for anything, and an agreement designed to be abandoned in week six tends to produce a build designed the same way. The commitment runs in both directions, which is worth saying out loud.

sections.h2: When a cheap template is honestly the right answer.
paras: The usual version of this advice asks whether you enjoy fiddling with software on a Sunday. Here is a better test, and it has nothing to do with temperament.

Look at where last year's work came from. If the truthful answer is two general contractors, a few property managers and a brother-in-law, then search is not how your business arrives, and paying anybody to improve it is buying a cure for a condition you do not have. Put something small and cheap up, keep the phone number correct on it, and spend the difference on a vehicle.

The same holds if you are three years from handing the place on, or if you are already turning work away and would rather keep your evenings than fill them. We would sooner set that out here than discover it together in month four.

pages.townPara: DuPage held 932,877 people at the 2020 Census, second-most of any county in Illinois, and hardly one of them thinks of themselves as living in DuPage. They live in a village with a name on the water tower. Three of those villages — Glen Ellyn, Wheaton and Lombard — have pages of their own on this site, and the builds behind them are identical in structure and nothing alike in content. That is the whole trick at this scale. The frame is the same everywhere in the county. What goes inside it is decided by your trade and by which roads your customers come off.

crmCallout.heading: The site collects names. Something has to hold on to them.
crmCallout.para: Three letters that only ever meant somewhere to keep what you know about the people who pay you. A site without one hands every enquiry straight back to a phone and a memory. On Growth, $500 a month after a one-time $500, the two are a single build rather than two purchases — the form fill becomes a record, the booking becomes an appointment, and the invoice is produced from that same entry instead of typed out again elsewhere. Foundation stops at the front door, which is frequently the right place to stop first.

cta.heading: Six finished builds, and the quickest way to judge any of this.
cta.para: Open two of them and decide whether they read as one design wearing different colors. Then call (331) 291-7400 and describe the business — the reply comes from whoever would be doing the building.

faqs.q: How long from agreeing to being live?
faqs.a: About a month is normal, and the pace is set by how fast things come back from you rather than by the building. The piece that can run long is anything held in an account somebody else controls — a domain parked with a developer who no longer answers email, a profile verified inside a former employee's inbox. That is precisely why it gets started in week one.

faqs.q: If we part ways, who ends up with what?
faqs.a: The domain, the Google Business Profile and the customer list were registered to you at the start, so all three simply stay where they already are. The pages were built for your business and nothing is held hostage against them. Put that same question to anybody else you are considering, because the answer to it is most of what you need to know.

faqs.q: We trade outside Glen Ellyn, Wheaton and Lombard. Does that change anything?
faqs.a: Not the build and not the figure. Those three have pages of their own because we know them well enough to write about them honestly, and everywhere else in the county gets the same work without the essay attached. Say where you trade when you call and the search side gets aimed at the right places.

pages.formHeading: Describe the business in three lines.
pages.formSub: What you sell, who buys it, and the question you answer on the phone most often. That is enough for a straight answer and a number.

pages.title: Local SEO in DuPage County, IL | Project Knox
pages.metaDescription: Local SEO in DuPage County, IL. How relevance, distance and prominence order the map, why you rank in one town but not the next, and what can't be promised.
pages.h1: Local SEO in DuPage County, IL, and why you rank in one town and not the next one over.
pages.lede: This is the part of the job almost nobody has ever had explained to them properly. It is not mysterious. It is three factors, and once you can name them the rest of this stops being infuriating.

sections.h2: Google names three things, and everything else sits underneath them.
paras: Google says openly that local results are ordered on relevance, distance and prominence. Relevance is how closely what you are matches what got typed. Distance is how far you sit from wherever the search was made. Prominence is how well known the business is, on its own site and everywhere else.

Nearly every question an owner has about local search turns out to be a question about one of those three, asked without the vocabulary for it. Why does a shop halfway across the county beat me. Why did things slip after somebody changed a category. Why does my position move when I drive somewhere. Each has a dull, answerable cause.
Two of the three can be worked on directly. The third cannot be worked on at all, and pretending otherwise is where most of the money in this industry quietly goes.

sections.h2: Distance is measured from the person, not from the county.
paras: This is the one that confuses everybody and it is worth reading twice. The map does not rank businesses for a place. It ranks them for a point — wherever the phone was standing at the moment somebody searched.

Which means there is no single answer to where do I rank. You rank one way from your own parking lot and another way from four miles up the road, and both of those results are real. An owner checking from behind the counter is looking at the most flattering version in existence, and a competitor across town is looking at an equally honest one that happens to say the opposite.

It also means nobody wins a county. Somebody searching from one end of DuPage and somebody searching from the other are having two separate conversations with the same search engine, and expecting one business to sit on top of both is expecting the map to do the one thing it was built not to do.

sections.h2: So the useful question is which searches are reachable from where you stand.
paras: The building cannot be moved. What can be done is to be truthful about the radius and then take everything inside it, rather than spending a year on results that were never available to begin with.

For a place with a counter, that radius is smaller than owners want and wider than they fear. For a business that travels to the customer, the arithmetic differs — the listing hides the address and publishes the towns covered instead, and distance is weighed against that area rather than against a storefront. It is not a loophole and it will not put you everywhere.

For anybody working across a broad slice of the county, the answer is more pages rather than more pins. One profile, one location, and writing that speaks properly about each place you genuinely serve.

sections.h2: Relevance is mostly the category, and the category is mostly ignored.
paras: The primary category on a Google Business Profile decides which searches you are eligible to appear in at all. Not how high — whether. It is the most consequential field in the entire listing, and it is usually chosen once, quickly, by whoever happened to set the thing up.

Beneath it sit the secondary categories, the service entries and the wording of every page on the site. There is nothing to game here and no trick being withheld. It is a slow, literal business of using the words your customers use, in enough places, often enough that nothing important has to be inferred.

sections.h2: Prominence is the slow one, and most of it is other people's doing.
paras: Prominence is how known you are. Reviews are the visible portion, and the pattern counts for more than the total — a listing gaining a few every month reads very differently from one that gained forty some years back and has been still ever since.

The rest is everything said about you in places you do not control. A directory entry, a chamber listing, a supplier's page, a local write-up, a mention with no link attached at all. None of it is for sale, and any of it that is for sale is not worth owning.

What can be done is to keep the asking automatic behind finished work, answer everything that arrives in your own voice, and make certain the details published about you agree with each other wherever they appear. Then it accumulates, slowly, in the direction you wanted.

sections.h2: What goes in writing, and what never will.
paras: Placement in local results is not sold by Google, so it cannot be sold by us either. A guarantee about a position on that map is a promise concerning somebody else's product.
Here is the standing arrangement offered in its place.
bullets: The profile worked on every month rather than opened when something breaks — categories, services, photographs, hours, posts
A review request behind every finished job, and every review that lands answered
One page written or rewritten each month, chosen from the words people really used to reach you
The published details about you kept identical everywhere they appear
Page speed and dead links watched, because a page that quietly breaks quietly stops being shown
A written account of what changed and what moved, sent in the flat months as well as the good ones

sections.h2: How long it takes, and how to tell without fooling yourself.
paras: Profile work can register within weeks, because completing categories, services and photographs hands the search engine facts it was already hunting for. Pages are slower — three months before there is anything fair to judge, and longer wherever several established businesses are already competing for the same handful of positions.

Checking it by searching for yourself is close to useless, for the reason set out further up. Read what the profile itself reports instead: how many people called, asked for directions or tapped through to the site, and whether those move the right way across a quarter rather than across a week.

pages.townPara: DuPage covers 336 square miles and holds 932,877 people, which reads like one market and behaves like several dozen. Nobody stands in a place called DuPage County. They stand on a street in a village, and the map answers them from there — which is how a business ends up being the obvious first choice at one end of Butterfield Road and effectively invisible at the other. That is not a fault in your listing and no amount of spending will argue with it. It is geography doing what geography does across a county this wide, and the work is to be unmissable inside the part of it you can genuinely reach.

crmCallout.heading: A result you cannot measure is a result you cannot manage.
crmCallout.para: The place customer information lives — which is the entire meaning of those three letters — turns out to be the only honest scoreboard any of this has. It records where each new customer said they came from, so whether the search work is paying stops being judged by whether the phone felt busy in March. Growth carries it at $500 a month after a one-time $500. If calls are already arriving and ringing out while everybody is working, round-the-clock answering is a separate $100 a month.

cta.heading: Read pages that were written the way this describes.
cta.para: Knox Pops is a chiropractic practice we built the whole way through, down to how each page is named and worded. Read two of them, then call (331) 291-7400 and we will look at what Google is currently publishing about you while you are still on the line.

faqs.q: Why do we show up when I search from the shop but not from my house?
faqs.a: Because distance is counted from the phone rather than from the business, so both of those results are genuine. Searching from your own counter produces the kindest version of the map there is, which is why it is a poor way to check anything. The reporting inside the profile is better, and so is asking a customer what came up for them.

faqs.q: Can you get us ranking across the whole county?
faqs.a: No, and neither can anyone else, because the map answers every searcher from wherever they happen to be. What is achievable is winning the searches made inside a radius you can actually serve, and deserving to be found for each place you genuinely work. A promise covering a whole county is a promise about something the search engine does not offer.

faqs.q: Which matters more, the Google profile or the website?
faqs.a: The profile drives the map, the website drives the list of links beneath it, and each leans on the other. If only one could be done, the profile would go first for most trades — it is quicker and it does more work. The site is what turns a listing into a booking, and it is also the half of the pair you own outright.

faqs.q: What does having the search work done properly come to?
faqs.a: It lives inside Foundation at $250 a month after a one-time $250, alongside the site, the email, the profile and the booking page. Growth at $500 a month after $500 adds the automatic review requests and the records they write into. No separate retainer arrives later, and no advertising budget is being quietly assumed underneath the figure.

faqs.q: We cover most of the county from one address. What should we expect?
faqs.a: Strong results near home, thinner ones as the miles add up, and a real ceiling somewhere between the two. Getting past it is a matter of pages and prominence rather than wishing at the map — write properly about each area you serve, become known in them, and accept that a competitor sitting four miles closer to a given searcher starts with an advantage there is no arguing with.

pages.formHeading: Name the search you want to win.
pages.formSub: Say what you sell and how far you are willing to drive for it, and we will come back with what stands between you and that result.

pages.title: CRM for DuPage County Businesses, IL | Project Knox
pages.metaDescription: The CRM for DuPage County, IL businesses. Booking, invoicing, follow-up, payments, expenses, accounting sync and monthly reports built as one system, not four.
pages.h1: The CRM for a DuPage County, IL business — one system in place of four that never speak.
pages.lede: Those three letters only ever meant somewhere to keep what you know about the people who pay you. This page walks the whole of ours, part by part, because the argument for it is not any single piece — it is that every piece was built as one thing. It comes with Growth at $500 a month plus a one-time $500.

sections.h2: Four subscriptions, four logins, and not one of them knows what the others did.
paras: Businesses at this stage are rarely disorganized. They have solved each problem separately, and solved it well. There is a booking app, because the phone became a bottleneck. There is a card reader keeping its own history. There is an email tool somebody set up to send a newsletter twice in 2023. There is accounting software, and somewhere among all four sits a spreadsheet holding whatever none of them would hold.

Each of those is a decent product. The trouble is the seams between them. One customer exists four times under four spellings, the payment sits somewhere the appointment cannot see it, and no plain question can be answered without three tabs and some arithmetic — how much has she spent with us, when was she last in, what does she still owe.

Keeping four products agreeing with each other is a job with no end and no output. It produces nothing, it happens on a Sunday, and it is the most common reason an owner tells us they gave up on records altogether.
What gets built instead is one record for each person with everything hanging off it. That sentence is the entire product. The eight sections below are only what becomes possible once it is true.

sections.h2: Appointment booking, and what an appointment is worth as a record.
paras: Booking is where the record begins, so what the booking captures matters. Each one arrives carrying a name, a number, the service chosen, the time and how that person found the page — and all five attach to the customer permanently rather than to that one Tuesday.

Underneath sits the Google Calendar you already carry. Block a morning out for something private and those hours stop being offered to anybody. Nothing gets copied across, because a second diary never comes into being to be copied to.

The confirmation then goes out by itself, and you learn about the eleven o'clock booking over coffee the next morning. For a business working across several towns, the quietly valuable part is travel time — set once as a buffer, so the page stops cheerfully promising a nine and a nine-thirty at addresses twenty minutes apart.

sections.h2: Invoicing, and the week it usually loses.
paras: The invoice is assembled out of the appointment already sitting in the system, so customer, date, service and price turn up filled in. You adjust whatever changed on the day and send it, by text or by email, with a link on it that takes a card.

Anything already paid comes off automatically — a deposit taken at booking is not a separate conversation, it is a line on the same document. Invoices run in sequence too, which sounds like nothing at all until the first time an accountant asks for a list with no gaps in it.

What replaces the shoebox is one screen holding everything outstanding with an age against each line, and reminders leaving on a schedule you set, in wording you approved. Which means nobody has to make the phone call that sours a perfectly good customer over a small amount of money.

sections.h2: The enquiry that never turned into work.
paras: Cold-lead follow-up is the part owners are most sceptical of and the part that most often covers the cost of the plan, so it is worth being exact about what it actually is.

Every enquiry gets a record whether or not it became a job — the call, the form, the message, the person who asked a price across the counter. Nothing is discarded for failing to convert. Anything left unanswered stays visible until somebody deals with it, and anything that simply went quiet receives one short note some weeks later saying the price still stands and there is room, with a sentence making plain you will leave them alone if the timing is wrong.

We are not going to attach a percentage to how many come back, because we do not have one and neither does anybody who quotes you one. What is certain is that the list does not currently exist inside your business, so the loss has never appeared on any report, which is exactly why it has been permitted to carry on.

sections.h2: The three messages, and the line we hold to on them.
paras: One message the day before an appointment. A thank-you shortly after they leave, carrying the review request with it. A check-in at whatever interval your trade runs on — six weeks, six months, every March. Each gets written once, in your words, and afterwards leaves with the correct name and time already inside it.
The reminder pays first and it pays quietly, in appointments that simply happen rather than in anything you could point at afterwards.

There is a limit we keep to here, and it deserves stating, because automation is the part of our own product we are most careful about. Nothing goes out that you have not read and approved. Nothing goes out more often than a person would send it. And only two things in this entire arrangement run without a human deciding — the round-the-clock answering and the review replies, both named, both priced, both optional. Everything else is your own words on a timer.

sections.h2: Money in and money out, written down in the same place.
paras: Card at the counter, a link inside a text, a deposit taken online at midnight, an order placed on the site — the route stops mattering, because all four land on the record of whoever paid, attached to the job that produced them.

Going the other way, what you spend is recorded beside what you take. Photograph a receipt where you stand — parts, fuel, materials, whatever had to be bought mid-job at eight in the morning, the advertising currently running — and it gets a date, a category and a job attached to it before you are back in the vehicle.

Those two habits together are what turn last month felt alright into a figure. A business measuring only one of the two directions is guessing at the other, and guessing is how an owner ends up unable to say which of the work is genuinely worth doing.

sections.h2: The accounting sync, and why it matters more than which software you use.
paras: Invoices, payments and expenses are handed to QuickBooks, or to whichever package your bookkeeper prefers, arriving already sorted. A monthly close turns into a review rather than a reconstruction.

This does not replace your accounting. It sits in front of it. The accounting package is where a year gets assembled and filed; the ledger is where the work happens, day after day, and that half is currently being run on a paper diary, a terminal and an inbox in most businesses we meet.

We configure the sync, and if your bookkeeper would rather decide the categories herself, that is a shorter conversation than you would expect. You keep your accountant, your filing habits and your fiscal year exactly as they are.

sections.h2: One page arrives on the first, and nobody has to remember to open it.
paras: It comes by email rather than waiting behind a login. That is deliberate. Anything requiring you to remember it is competing with the rest of your Tuesday, and losing.
bullets: What came in, broken out by service
What went out, by category, set against the month before
Who has drifted past their usual interval, by name and by number
First-time customers set against returning ones
Everything unpaid, and how long it has been unpaid
Where new customers said they found you

sections.h2: What it costs, what it switches off, and what Foundation will not do.
paras: The CRM belongs to Growth: $500 a month, plus $500 once at the start, and that figure carries the website standing in front of it rather than sitting on top of it.

Foundation, at $250 a month with $250 at the start, includes none of this page. Better you read that here than be told it on a call. Foundation is the being-found half — the site, the profile, booking on your calendar, email at your domain and the search work — and for a great many businesses it is the correct first purchase.

A year settled in advance takes 15 percent off either, so $2,550 or $5,100 across the twelve months, which reads as $212.50 and $425 a month, with the build billed on its own line. The extras are $100 a month for round-the-clock phone answering and $130 a month for automated Google review replies, and either sits on either plan. Anything beyond all that is quoted to the job and put in writing first.

One fair objection deserves a straight answer. You could assemble something resembling this out of four separate subscriptions, and depending on what you chose it might come to less per month than Growth does. What you would be buying back is the seams — the exports, the double entry, the evening every quarter spent making two histories agree with each other — and whether that trade is worth making depends entirely on what an evening of yours is worth.

Booking, confirmations, reminders, thank-yous and review requests
Invoicing, deposits, card payments and one screen of what is outstanding
Chasing for the customers who drifted, and for the prices quoted that nobody ever came back on

pages.townPara: A DuPage customer is rarely a neighbour in the old sense of the word. Roosevelt Road, Butterfield and North Avenue run the county from east to west, I-355 and IL 53, 59 and 83 run it the other way, and Wheaton sits in the middle of the arrangement as the county seat. What that does to an owner is produce a customer who lives off one of those roads, works off another and passes your door on a third. She is not a regular on anybody's street. She is a regular in your records or she is nobody at all, which is what a ledger is for in a county that does most of its living at thirty-five miles an hour.

crmCallout.heading: It is your ledger, in your name, from the first week.
crmCallout.para: The customer list, the domain and the Google Business Profile go into your accounts at the start rather than into ours. If we ever stop working together, all three stay precisely where they already are, and the names export into a plain file that any other system will read, with no notice period and nobody ringing to talk you round. It is worth having in writing, because the day an owner finds out otherwise is always the worst possible day to find it out.

cta.heading: Nothing behind this link is a screenshot, so go and use it.
cta.para: The demo is a working CRM with a year of somebody's trading already loaded into it. Book something into the calendar, raise an invoice against yourself, log an expense, open the overdue list and decide whether it resembles your year. Then either the form below or (331) 291-7400 gets you a person.

faqs.q: Could we not just buy a booking app and an invoicing app separately?
faqs.a: You could, and for some businesses that is the right call. If you only need two of the eight things described on this page, buying two products is cheaper and simpler than buying ours, and we would say so. It stops being the right call at the point where somebody in the building has to keep them agreeing with each other, because that job never finishes and nobody ever budgets for it.

faqs.q: Which of the tools we pay for now would this actually switch off?
faqs.a: Normally the booking app, the invoicing tool, whatever records the card reader keeps on its own, and the spreadsheet that was holding the customer list. Accounting software stays exactly where it is. So does anything clinical, like the system a practice charts in. We would rather tell you what to keep than pretend this replaces everything you own.

faqs.q: How much of it has to be running before it is worth anything?
faqs.a: Booking and invoicing on their own justify it for most trades, and both are live within the first few weeks. Follow-up and the reports need a few months of history behind them before they say anything useful, which is worth hearing now so that month two does not feel like a letdown. Nothing has to be switched on at once.

faqs.q: Does the price move if we have more staff, more customers or more locations?
faqs.a: No. $500 a month with a one-time $500 is the figure whatever the headcount, however many records the ledger holds and however many towns you serve. Nobody gets billed by the person, and there is no larger tier being kept in reserve, because Foundation and Growth are the only two things on the price list.

faqs.q: Who configures all of this? Does it land on us?
faqs.a: We do it. Services and prices loaded, the three messages drafted in your words for you to approve, payments connected, the accounting sync mapped, your existing customers imported. What you supply is decisions and an hour of attention. The single hard gate is the phone answering extra, which stays dark until the recording disclosures your state expects have been set up, and that is our job too.

pages.formSub: List what handles your booking, your money, your messages and your records, and we will say plainly which parts this would replace and which you ought to keep.

pages.title: Online Booking & Payments, DuPage County IL | Project Knox
pages.metaDescription: Online booking and payments for DuPage County, IL businesses. Deposits, cards on file, recurring billing, no-shows, refunds, and where the money goes and when.
pages.h1: Online booking and payments in DuPage County, IL, and what really happens to the money.
pages.lede: Taking a card is the easy part. The questions worth answering are which method suits which job, what a deposit does about people who do not turn up, and how long it is before any of it is in your bank.

sections.h2: There are four ways to be paid, and the wrong one costs you weekly.
paras: Every trade uses some mixture of these, and the mixture is usually arrived at by accident rather than chosen.
bullets: Paid in full when the booking is made — suits anything short, flat-priced and delivered on the same visit
A deposit at booking with the balance later — suits anything long, expensive, or easy to walk away from
A card held on file and charged once the work is finished — suits a route, a repeat visit, or a job whose final figure moves
An invoice sent afterwards with a link on it — suits a customer who is a business, or a number that depends on what got found

sections.h2: What a deposit is genuinely for.
paras: It is not a punishment and it is not a cash-flow manoeuvre. A deposit is a filter, and it does its filtering before the cost has landed on you rather than afterwards.

The thing being protected is the slot, which is the only inventory a service business has. It cannot be stored, it cannot be marked down later and it cannot be sold to two people. An hour nobody came to is not a missed sale — it is an hour that has already been spent.

So you decide the amount, which services carry one, and how long before the appointment it stops being refundable. All three sit on the page where somebody reads them before booking rather than after missing. The refund window is the part most businesses leave out, and it is the part that keeps a deposit from reading like a trap.

sections.h2: A card on file is how a recurring account stops being a monthly errand.
paras: Weekly accounts, monthly retainers, a maintenance agreement, anything billed on repeat — those are the arrangements that quietly eat an evening a month in reminders, checking and small awkward messages.

Held properly, a card is charged when the work is done, the receipt goes straight out, and nobody has to be asked for anything. The card details themselves stay with the payment processor rather than with you or with us, which is both the correct arrangement and the one that keeps the obligation off your desk.

Two things go wrong with repeat billing and both have plain handling. Cards expire, so the customer hears about it before the failure instead of after it. And charges occasionally decline for reasons that have nothing to do with the person paying, so a failed one lands on a list to be tried again rather than disappearing into a report nobody opens.

sections.h2: The cancellation is not the problem. The silence is.
paras: A cancellation with warning is close to a gift. Somebody told you, the hour is back on the market, and there is still time to do something with it. The expensive version is the one nobody mentions until the appointment time has come and gone.

Two mechanics handle most of it. A cancellation window stated plainly, with whatever charge attaches to a late one written in the same sentence — people accept this everywhere else in their lives and object to it far less than owners expect. And a waiting list, so that when an hour does come free, everybody who wanted that day hears about it by text while it is still worth something to them.

The record does work here too. A customer who has missed three appointments is no longer a memory or a grudge. It is a fact on a screen, and it is the only reasonable basis on which anybody decides to ask that particular person for a deposit next time.

sections.h2: Where the money goes, and when.
paras: Nobody explains this part, so here it is in order. A card is authorized at the moment it is charged, which is the moment the customer sees it leave. It then settles into your own bank account on the payment processor's schedule rather than instantly, and it arrives as a batch covering several transactions instead of one line per sale.

Which is precisely why the attaching matters. When a payout lands on a Thursday you can see which jobs made it, because every payment stayed fastened to the appointment and the customer that produced it. Without that, a batch deposit is a number you accept and cannot explain.

The account is yours. The processor charges its own rate for handling the card, which is a matter between you and them, and we neither add a percentage on top nor take a share of anything you take in. Our bill is the monthly plan figure and nothing besides.

sections.h2: Refunds, disputes and the awkward afternoon.
paras: Sooner or later somebody wants their money back, and how well that goes depends almost entirely on how quickly you can see what happened.

A refund is issued against the original payment, in part or in full, and stays fastened to the same record, so the history reads as one account of events rather than two that contradict each other. If it escalates and the customer disputes the charge with their own bank, what settles it is evidence — the booking, the confirmation that went out, the terms agreed to on the page, the invoice.
Nobody puts that in a brochure. It is one of the better reasons all of this was built as a single system, and you will be grateful for it exactly once, on an afternoon you had not planned for.

sections.h2: What each half costs.
paras: Booking that writes to your Google Calendar is Foundation work — $250 a month, and $250 once at the outset, together with the site, the email at your own domain, the profile and the local search behind it.

Taking money — deposits, cards on file, orders placed online, invoices with a link — belongs to Growth, at $500 a month after a one-time $500, together with the automatic messages and the records all of it writes into. Twelve months paid in advance takes 15 percent off either, so $2,550 or $5,100, with the build charged separately.
There is nothing else on the bill. No transaction fee payable to us, no minimum volume, and no third plan being held back for businesses that happen to take more money than average.

pages.townPara: Two things cross this county without belonging to any one town: the Metra Union Pacific West line and the Illinois Prairie Path, one carrying people to work and the other carrying them for the pleasure of it. Both are a reminder that a good deal of DuPage life happens away from home and away from a desk, in the gaps between where somebody has been and where they have to be next. Arrangements get made in those gaps — on a platform, in a parked car, in the twenty minutes before the next thing starts. A page that takes both the booking and the payment is working through every one of them.

crmCallout.heading: A payment is only useful while it stays attached to a person.
crmCallout.para: Everything described here writes into the same ledger, which is all those three letters have ever meant — the place your customer information ends up. Six months along, that record answers the questions a card reader never could: how often she books, what she has spent altogether, what is still open, whether she has missed one before. It is part of Growth, which runs $500 monthly after $500 at the start, and it is the same system as the booking page rather than a second thing to keep in step.

cta.heading: Pay for something in a demo and follow the money.
cta.para: Knox Guac is a working taqueria we built with ordering and payment switched on. Put an order through it, watch the confirmation arrive, then look at the record it created on the other side of the counter. When it makes sense, (331) 291-7400 reaches a person.

faqs.q: Does the money come to us or through you?
faqs.a: To you. The payment account is in your name and the funds settle into your bank on the processor's schedule. We do not stand between a business and its revenue, we hold nothing, and we take no percentage of what you bring in. Our bill is the monthly plan figure and that is the whole of it.

faqs.q: Can we ask for a deposit on some services and not others?
faqs.a: You can, and it is usually the sensible arrangement. Set it per service — a deposit on the long, costly or easily abandoned work, and nothing at all on the short visits where it would only add friction. The amount, the services it applies to and the refund window are yours to decide, and any of them can change whenever a season or a price does.

faqs.q: Half our customers still pay cash. Does that break something?
faqs.a: Not in the slightest, and nothing here removes a payment method. Cash and checks get recorded against the same job in a couple of taps, so the month still adds up and the customer's history stays complete. The point is adding a route to be paid, not closing one you already have.

pages.formHeading: Tell us how the money reaches you now.
pages.formSub: Cash, checks, a card reader, an invoice written at night, or all four at once. Say which, and we will show you the same week handled in one place.
